rendered: The review does not actually recommend tens of nanometres for low-diffusivity oxides such as ZrO2. Its recommendation is thinner. For the cost-effective, scalable coating materials that have very low lithium-ion diffusivity, it gives a maximum coating thickness of about ∼10 nm[1]. Its calculations point the same way: ideal thicknesses for these surface coatings should be below ten nanometers[2]. The reason is kinetic. Lithium-ion diffusion time depends on the diffusion length and the diffusivity, and for these low-diffusivity oxides longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers[3]. Thick layers also carry a chemical risk: inert oxides such as ZrO2 or Al2O3 may react with lithium ions and form secondary phases[4] (for example Li2ZrO3), resulting in capacity fading issue[5]. The tens-of-nanometre figure appears only as a description of current practice, not as a recommendation: The reported coating thickness in literature, in most cases, is in the tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled by easily scalable processes[6].
